problem: Model-based planning and control needs a known map, but building a globally consistent geometric map online from onboard sensors is expensive and brittle. It fails with shiny, thin or transparent objects and under strong ambient light. End-to-end visuomotor policies avoid mapping, but they are sample-inefficient, ignore dynamics (macro-actions or direct velocity regression) and give jerky, inefficient control on real robots.
motivation: A ground robot in an unseen cluttered indoor building has to reach a relative point goal using only a monocular RGB camera, and it must be deployable directly from simulation. The key observation is that learning only needs to decide 'where to go' from visual semantics such as doorways, hallways and obstacles. The known dynamics model and a feedback controller can handle 'how to go' smoothly and robustly, which also absorbs the dynamics mismatch between simulation and the real robot.
key_idea: A CNN maps the current RGB image, the relative goal and the current speed to a single dynamically-meaningful waypoint (x, y, θ). A cubic-spline planner plus an LQR tracking controller turns that waypoint into smooth, feasible controls. The CNN is supervised by collision-aware MPC waypoints computed from known training maps, so no human labeling is needed.
insight:
Factorizing the problem so that learning predicts only the next waypoint, while model-based control executes it, makes the learning problem much easier than regressing velocities.
- Against an E2E network trained on the same expert trajectories (Table 1), success is 80.65% vs 58.06%, time 11.52 s vs 19.16 s, and jerk 0.39 vs 8.07 m/s³, which is expert-level smoothness.
- Adding a smoothing loss to E2E reduced jerk but significantly cut success, which shows that jointly learning accurate and smooth control is hard.
- Heavy image and perspective augmentation matters a lot: success rises from 47.94% without it to 80.65%, and it enables sim-to-real transfer.
- The LQR feedback absorbs the crude Dubins-car model mismatch on the real TurtleBot, with about 4 cm tracking accuracy.
- Real depth sensors miss shiny, thin and black objects and degrade in sunlight, so the RGB-D mapping baseline drops from 97.85% in sim to 40% in the real world.
- Design details also matter. The waypoint heading θ is treated as a free degree of freedom rather than line-of-sight, which gives richer collision-free splines. The expert's cubic obstacle penalty keeps trajectories away from obstacles, which the authors found makes waypoints easier to learn.
method: Perception CNN: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 (fine-tuned) encodes a 224×224 RGB image. A downsampling conv is followed by 5 FC layers (128 units, 20% dropout), with the relative goal (x*, y*) and current (v, ω) concatenated. The network regresses a waypoint ŵ = (x̂, ŷ, θ̂) with MSE loss (Adam, lr 1e-4, batch 64, 35K iterations, weight decay 1e-6).

Spline planner: models the robot as a 3-D Dubins car (ẋ = v cos φ, ẏ = v sin φ, φ̇ = ω, with bounded v and ω). It fits third-order polynomial splines from the current state and speed to the waypoint by solving linear equations, giving smooth, dynamically feasible state and control trajectories over horizon H.

LQR tracking controller: the dynamics are linearized around the spline trajectory to compute feed-forward and feedback gains {k, K}. Controls u = K(z − z*) + k run for H = 1.5 s (0.5 s in the dynamic-obstacle experiment), then a new image triggers replanning. This is a purely reactive loop with no memory.

MPC expert supervision: uses known training maps. The per-step cost is max{0, λ1 − d_obs}³ + λ2·d_goal² (d_goal is the FMM geodesic distance), with λ1 = 0.3 m. Each step solves a receding-horizon problem over H1 = 6 s by sampling waypoints in the ground-projected field of view and scoring their spline trajectories. The result is collision-free, dynamically feasible waypoint labels with no human annotation.

Domain randomization: during training, random blur, dropped pixels, superpixels, noise, and changes to saturation, sharpness, contrast and brightness are applied with imgaug. Field-of-view and camera-tilt perspective distortions are also applied, which is key for sim-to-real under camera pitch changes and lighting.

setting.backbone: ResNet-50 (ImageNet-pretrained, fine-tuned) + 5-layer MLP waypoint head; model-based cubic-spline planner + LQR controller (not learned)
setting.model_size: ResNet-50 + 5×128 FC layers (parameter count not stated)
setting.training_data: 125K data points (image, relative goal, speed, optimal waypoint) generated by the MPC expert on scans of 2 S3DIS buildings, with heavy image and perspective augmentation; no real-world data
setting.observation: single monocular RGB image (224×224) + goal position in robot frame + current linear/angular speed; exact robot state assumed
setting.action_space: predicted waypoint (x, y, θ) → cubic spline → LQR continuous linear/angular velocity, replanned every H = 1.5 s
setting.simulator: custom renderer over S3DIS (Stanford Large-Scale 3D Indoor Spaces) building scans
setting.privileged: perfect state/odometry assumed (exact pose in sim, onboard TurtleBot odometry in the real world); GT map used only at training time for expert labels

results: In simulation, LB-WayPtNav reaches 80.65% success vs 58.06% for an E2E velocity-regression policy trained on the same expert data. It is also faster (11.52 s vs 19.16 s) and far smoother (jerk 0.39 vs 8.07 m/s³, near the expert's 0.36). It trails the depth-based mapping planners that use perfect simulated depth (memoryless 86.56%, with memory 97.85%). On a real TurtleBot 2 in unseen buildings, zero-shot sim-to-real, it succeeds in 95% of trials vs 50% for E2E, 40% for RTAB-Map RGB-D mapping and 0% for memoryless mapping. The mapping baselines fail because the depth sensor misses shiny, thin and black objects and degrades in sunlight.
limitations: Purely reactive, with no memory. It fails when too close to obstacles or when backtracking is needed, which makes it unsuitable for long-range tasks.
Assumes perfect state estimation/odometry and a static environment. Dynamic obstacles are shown only in a single qualitative demo.
Small-scale evaluation: 2 training buildings, 1 test building (185 episodes) and 20 real trials. It fails when real object appearance differs too much from simulation.
